Every fix in this lab so far has come from tracing a chain of dependencies that wasn't
visible until something broke: volume meaning different things for different models, a
mean-based price sitting next to a P90-based cost, a "risk score" that only touches three
of the five models. This page draws that map out up front.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the diagrams
**Solid arrows** are real dependencies — implemented in `comparator.qmd`'s code today, and
you can move the corresponding slider and watch the number change. **Dashed arrows** are
*conceptual* links — relationships that plausibly should exist given how the reference doc
and the rest of this site talk about risk and variability, but which the model currently
treats as independent sliders. They're flagged here as a map of where the model is
simplified, not a defect list.
:::

The full picture was one dense diagram; it's split into two smaller ones below — **drivers**
(the qualitative/shared inputs) and **computation** (how those drivers turn into price, cost
and margin) — so each stays readable on its own.

## The wider view: a causal loop diagram

The four diagrams above are *calling sequences* — acyclic maps of how one slider's value
propagates into a number on the bar chart. They deliberately stop at the edge of the
spreadsheet. But the business those numbers describe is not acyclic: price feeds margin,
margin funds capability, capability raises the value delivered, and that in turn changes
what a customer will pay. Those are **feedback loops**, and they're invisible in a DAG.

This last diagram is a proper **causal loop diagram (CLD)**. It doesn't correspond to any
code in `comparator.qmd` — nothing here moves when you drag a slider. It's a model of the
operating environment the lab sits inside, drawn to show where the reinforcing and
balancing pressures actually are.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading a causal loop diagram
Each arrow carries a **polarity**. A **`+`** means the two variables move *the same way*
(more of the cause → more of the effect, all else equal); a **`−`** means they move
*opposite* ways. Trace a loop and count the `−` signs: an **even** number (including zero)
makes it a **reinforcing (R)** loop — a virtuous or vicious cycle that compounds; an
**odd** number makes it a **balancing (B)** loop — one that pushes back toward equilibrium.
Node colour groups variables by domain: <span style="color:#4a6fa5">**customer**</span>,
<span style="color:#3f7d54">**commercial**</span>,
<span style="color:#c08a3e">**delivery / adoption**</span>,
<span style="color:#c0504d">**cost**</span>, and
<span style="color:#7a5aa5">**market**</span>.
:::

### The loops, one at a time

| Loop | Type | Chain | What it means for pricing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1 · Value flywheel** | Reinforcing | value → willingness-to-pay → price → margin → reinvestment → value | The core case for value-based (M4/M5) pricing: capturing more of the value you create funds the capability that creates more value. Left unbalanced it compounds. |
| **R2 · Land & expand** | Reinforcing | value → trust → autonomy (L1→L5) → volume → proof → (trust / new engagements) → volume → value | Trust earned at low autonomy is what lets you move a customer up the tier ladder; each delivered task is a reference that widens the footprint. This is the growth engine the tier model is built around. |
| **B1 · Token-cost squeeze** | Balancing | volume × complexity → token consumption → P90 compute cost → margin (−) | Growth is not free: more volume and harder tasks push the *tail* of the cost distribution, which is exactly why the cost side is priced at P90, not the mean. |
| **B2 · Efficiency response** | Balancing | margin (−) → optimisation (−) → compute cost → margin | A thin margin creates pressure to optimise models and prompts, pulling compute cost back down — the self-correcting counterweight to B1. |
| **B3 · Value-share / churn cliff** | Balancing | value → aggressive value-share → perceived cost → churn risk → volume (−) | The renegotiation cliff from the M5 Outcome Designer, seen as a loop: the more value you capture, the more the customer feels the price, and past a point they walk. It caps how hard R1 can be pushed. |
| **B4 · Commoditisation** | Balancing | margin → competitor pressure ← market maturity → price (−) | Fat margins and a maturing market attract competitors whose pricing erodes yours — the long-run ceiling on any single deal's economics. |
| **B5 · Oversight capacity** | Balancing | volume → human-oversight hours → spare capacity (−) → volume | Agentic work still needs human oversight; as volume grows it consumes the very capacity needed to deliver it, unless autonomy (R2) raises the ceiling. |

The interesting tension is between the two reinforcing engines (R1, R2) and the four
balancing loops that constrain them. R1 says *capture more value*; B3 and B4 say *not too
much, or you'll lose the customer or the market*. R2 says *grow volume*; B1 and B5 say
*volume has a cost and a capacity ceiling*. A durable pricing strategy is essentially a
choice about which balancing loop you let bind first.

## Known gaps (dashed edges above)

These are places the model treats inputs as independent when a real pricing conversation
probably wouldn't — flagged here rather than fixed, since each is a judgement call about
how much realism this teaching tool needs versus how many more sliders it should have.

| Gap | What's missing |
|---|---|
| Task complexity → Token CoV | `m3Complexity` scales M3's *price*, but has no effect on either model's token-cost variability, even though a more complex task plausibly has a fatter-tailed token distribution too. |
| Risk score → per-unit risk premiums | The shared `riskScore` slider drives the generic overlay (M1, M2 T1, M4), but M2 Tier 2 and M3 have their own, entirely independent risk-premium sliders. Moving the shared risk score does nothing to them. |
| Token CoV / P90 → M5's floor | `token-distribution.qmd` explicitly teaches "set the floor on the P90/P95 cost, not a flat percentage" — but M5's actual floor is `0.8 × M4 base fee`, with no connection to any token-cost distribution at all. |
| Deployment tier → default recalibration | Switching tiers changes which models are *shown*, but doesn't adjust any default slider values — a Tier 3 (Digital Labor) scenario and a Tier 1 (Internal Use) scenario keep the same defaults even though the underlying engagement shape is usually very different. |
